screens.title: Introduction to systemd: Services and Targets
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of systemd and why it matters for day-to-day administration. Systemd is the init system that starts early in boot, manages services and sockets, evaluates dependencies, and maintains the journal of system events. You will learn the vocabulary systemd uses — units, service units, targets — and why those terms replace older runlevel concepts. We’ll also practice with systemctl commands to control services in the running session and to configure startup behavior for subsequent boots. Finally, we will create a small custom service so you see the full lifecycle: unit file, daemon reload, starting, enabling, and checking logs. This matters because most major distributions adopt systemd; competency with its commands and unit files is essential for reliably starting services, diagnosing failures, and automating startup behavior. By the end of the module you’ll be able to explain what a unit is, run basic systemctl workflows, and confidently handle common mistakes such as forgetting to run daemon-reload or editing package-provided unit files directly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Introduction

Introduction to systemd

A concise orientation to units, service control, targets, and practical workflows you will use every day as a sysadmin.

Systemd is more than an init program: it acts as the service manager, dependency resolver, and central logger. This module focuses on the concrete skills you need: recognizing unit types, using systemctl to control services, interpreting status output, reading the journal, and creating a simple unit file so your service runs across boots.

We emphasize hands-on practice and common pitfalls, like the difference between starting a service now and enabling it for future boots, and why you should avoid editing package-provided unit files directly.

In this lesson
Units, systemctl basics, targets, logs, and a small custom service lab.
Units
Service, socket, target, timer
Control
systemctl start/enable/status
Logs
journalctl for service logs
Visual Concept
systemd
manages units, resolves dependencies, and coordinates boot targets.
Units
unit files describe how services, mounts, sockets, and timers behave.
Targets
group units into boot states similar to legacy runlevels.
Explore Key Topics
Units and the unit file locations, practical systemctl commands for lifecycle management, and targets that define boot behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you must demonstrate. First, you will explain systemd's role and architecture, meaning you can describe why systemd runs early in boot and how it coordinates services and dependencies. A second objective is managing services with systemctl: you will start, stop, restart, reload, enable, and disable units reliably and understand the difference between the current running state and the enabled state for future boots. Third, you will identify common unit file types and locate unit files; you should be able to open a service unit and point out its sections and common directives. Fourth, you will understand targets and how they map to legacy runlevels so you can change the default target to a multi-user or graphical mode and explain rescue and emergency targets. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your mastery by performing the commands and explaining the results.

screens.title: What is systemd?
screens.narratorSegment: Systemd is the init system and service manager used by most modern Linux distributions to orchestrate boot, services, and system-wide resources. At boot, systemd is the first user-space process the kernel launches. It reads unit files, determines dependencies, and brings up resources in a dependency-aware, parallel fashion so boot is faster and more predictable than older sequential init scripts. Units are the core abstraction: each unit file declares a resource and how to manage it. Service units describe daemons and how to start and stop them. Other unit types include mount for filesystems, socket for socket-activated services, timer for scheduled tasks, and target for grouping units into a logical state. Why this matters: when you understand systemd's role you can trace a failed boot to the responsible unit, adjust dependencies to control order, and use uniform tools to inspect state. A common misconception is thinking systemd only starts services; in fact it also manages the journal, socket activation, device activation, and timers. Example: if a network target is marked After for a web service, systemd will delay starting the web service until network. target is reached. Key takeaway: treat units as first-class objects you can query, modify, and reason about to control system behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › What is systemd?
Core Concept

Systemd: init and service manager

Systemd starts early, reads unit files, resolves dependencies, and manages services, sockets, mounts, timers, and the journal.

Why it matters
Predictable parallel startup and a single control interface for service life cycles reduces time to recover from failures.
Common misconception
Systemd is not just a boot script runner; it provides socket activation, timers, and a centralized journal used for diagnostics.
Key Takeaway

Think in units and targets: unit files declare behavior, and systemd executes them in dependency order.

Unit Types Overview
service
Manages daemons and applications (example: httpd.service).
socket
Socket activation for on-demand services.
target
Groups units into a boot state, similar to runlevels.
timer
Schedules units at defined times instead of cron.
Concrete example
If a web service unit has After=network.target, systemd ensures the network target is reached before activating the web service, preventing startup failures due to missing network services.

screens.title: Units and unit file locations
screens.narratorSegment: A unit is the primary object systemd manages. Each unit has a type and a unit file that describes how to start, stop, and configure that resource. The most common type you will edit is the service unit. Unit files are plain text with INI-like sections, typically Unit, Service, and Install for services. Unit file locations signal ownership and persistence: package-provided units generally live under /usr/lib/systemd/system, while system-wide customizations and overrides belong under /etc/systemd/system. When both locations define the same unit name, files in /etc take precedence. This is important because editing files under /usr/lib risks losing changes when packages update; instead, create drop-in overrides or place your unit in /etc. When you change unit files you must run daemon-reload to tell systemd to pick up the edits; failing to do so is a common error. Concrete example: a service unit contains ExecStart to start the daemon and Restart to control auto-restart behavior. Misconception check: people sometimes think enabling a service writes a startup script; in reality it creates symlinks under the selected target directories so systemd starts that unit when the target is active. Key takeaway: edit or override units in /etc and always reload the daemon after changes.

keyIdea.text: Unit files define behavior; prefer /etc for overrides and remember daemon-reload after changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Units & Locations
Definition

Unit file anatomy

Service unit files usually contain three sections: Unit, Service, and Install. Unit holds metadata and dependencies, Service describes how to run the process, and Install controls target membership for enabling the unit.

Example unit excerpt
[Unit]
Description=My Custom Test Service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mytestservice.sh
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Best practice
Create overrides with systemctl edit or place unit files under /etc/systemd/system to persist changes.
Common mistake
Editing files in /usr/lib/systemd/system directly can be overwritten by package updates.
Locations
/usr/lib/systemd/system
Package-provided units; avoid editing here.
/etc/systemd/system
System administrator overrides and custom units; these take precedence.
Action
After editing a unit file run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so the systemd manager reads the new configuration.
Concrete example
If you add Restart=always to a service unit in /etc, run daemon-reload, then start the service to observe the behavior on failure.

screens.title: systemctl basics: start, stop, restart, reload
screens.narratorSegment: Systemctl is the primary tool for interacting with systemd. Use systemctl to change the current state of a unit and to alter whether it starts automatically in the future. The key commands you will use are start and stop to change the immediate running state, restart to stop and then start a service, and reload to request the service re-read its configuration without a full restart when supported. Another important pair is enable and disable: enable sets up the unit to start on matching targets after a reboot, and disable removes those startup links. A frequent confusion is treating start as persistent; starting a service affects only the current session — enabling controls future boots. Example scenario: you can start a web server to test a configuration change, and if it behaves correctly, enable it so it runs after reboot. Misconceptions often cause admins to forget enabling a service and be surprised after the next reboot. When reloading, check the service documentation to confirm it supports reload; otherwise use restart. Key takeaway: use start for immediate tests, enable for persistent startup, and daemon-reload whenever unit files change so systemctl acts on updated definitions.

keyIdea.title: Control vs Persistence
keyIdea.text: start/stop change the running state now; enable/disable control whether the unit runs after reboot.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › systemctl Basics
Comparison

Immediate commands vs persistent configuration

Immediate control
start, stop, restart, reload change the current runtime state of a unit.
Startup configuration
enable and disable control whether the unit will be started automatically by systemd during boot.
Concrete example
Start a service to test a change, then enable it only after confirming the behavior across restarts.
Common commands
sudo systemctl start servicename.service
sudo systemctl stop servicename.service
sudo systemctl restart servicename.service
sudo systemctl reload servicename.service
sudo systemctl enable servicename.service
sudo systemctl disable servicename.service
sudo systemctl status servicename.service
Misconception check
Enabling does not start a service immediately; start and enable are separate actions and both may be needed depending on your goal.

screens.title: Interpreting systemctl status output
screens.narratorSegment: When a service misbehaves, systemctl status is your first diagnostic tool. The status output summarizes whether a unit is active, its main PID, recent log lines forwarded from the journal, and runtime details such as memory usage. Learn to read three important pieces: the Active line shows state and timestamps, the Main PID line identifies the process you can inspect further, and the bottom log excerpt shows immediate errors and messages from the service or from systemd itself. Example: if status shows failed with a recent exit code and the log shows configuration parse errors, you know to inspect the unit's ExecStart and the service's configuration files. A common mistake is relying only on status; sometimes the status excerpt is too short. In that case use journalctl -u to view the full history. Also use systemctl show for machine-readable properties when you need environment variables or cgroup details. Practical tip: copy the unit name exactly and include the. service suffix for clarity when troubleshooting. Closing question: after reading status, what next step gives you the most evidence — checking journalctl for the full log or examining the unit file for misconfigured ExecStart arguments?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Reading status
Definition

systemctl status explained

The Active line tells you the unit's current state and whether it failed; the Main PID identifies the running process to inspect; the journal excerpt shows recent messages relevant to the failure.

If it shows failed
Use journalctl -u unitname to get the full log history and locate configuration or dependency errors.
Pro tip
Include the .service suffix when running status to avoid ambiguity, and copy the Main PID to inspect with ps or strace if necessary.
Example output
● mytestservice.service - My Custom Test Service
   Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/mytestservice.service; enabled)
   Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Tue 202X-XX-XX 12:34:56
  Process: 1234 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mytestservice.sh (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)

Oct 05 12:34:56 hostname mytestservice[1234]: configuration parse error: missing value
Next step
Run journalctl -u mytestservice.service to see full logs and timestamps that pinpoint the failing action or dependency.

screens.title: Using journalctl to read service logs
screens.narratorSegment: Journalctl is the central tool for viewing systemd's journal. For service troubleshooting, run journalctl with the -u flag followed by the unit name to see all entries for that service. You can limit output by time ranges or by following new entries in real time. For example, to see the most recent messages for a service you can run journalctl -u the service and then add --since to narrow to a timestamp range or -f to follow new lines. This helps when you restart a service and want to watch startup messages as they appear. A key point is that systemd aggregates logs from services and the kernel; journalctl gives you a unified timeline. Misconception: journalctl output can be large; use filtering flags and --no-pager to get machine-friendly output if you plan to pipe it. If you notice missing messages for a short-lived service, consider running journalctl -u with --since '5 minutes ago' immediately after a failure to capture ephemeral logs. Concrete example: to review only errors, pipe journalctl -u unitname --priority=err to focus on error-level messages. Closing thought: when in doubt, gather the journal as your primary evidence before editing unit files.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › journalctl
Process

Collecting useful log slices

Use journalctl -u unitname to focus on a single service. Add --since or --until to control the time window and -f to follow logs in real time during a restart test.

Filter example
To see recent errors: journalctl -u unitname --since "5 minutes ago" --priority=err
Example usage
sudo journalctl -u mytestservice.service --since "202X-10-05 12:00" --until "202X-10-05 12:10"
sudo journalctl -u mytestservice.service -f
sudo journalctl -u mytestservice.service --priority=err --no-pager
Why this helps
Filtered journal outputs let you pinpoint the failing step without wading through unrelated system noise.

screens.title: Targets and runlevel mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Targets offer a human-friendly way to express a set of units that should be active for a particular system state. They replace legacy runlevels with descriptive names like multi-user. target for non-graphical multi-user operation or graphical. target when a graphical session is desired. Rescue and emergency targets provide single-user and minimal states for recovery. Use systemctl get-default to see the default target the system boots into, and systemctl set-default to change it. Targets act as a collection point: enabling a target will pull in its WantedBy or Required units when the system reaches that target. A common misunderstanding is expecting targets to be services; instead they are grouping constructs — they do not run code but cause the units they reference to be started. Example: WantedBy=multi-user. target in a unit's Install section ensures the unit is started when multi-user. target becomes active. When troubleshooting boot state, examining which units a target requires and what failed during activation narrows the problem quickly. Key takeaway: change targets to alter boot behavior, but inspect unit dependencies to understand why a target fails to reach its desired state.

keyIdea.text: Targets group units for boot states; use get-default and set-default to control boot behavior and inspect WantedBy for startup membership.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Targets
Definition

Targets vs runlevels

Targets are named states that group units. They are not services themselves, but they cause member units to be started when the target becomes active.

multi-user.target
Non-graphical multi-user mode, like traditional runlevel 3.
graphical.target
Adds graphical session services on top of multi-user.
rescue.target
Single-user recovery mode for maintenance.
Commands & example
sudo systemctl get-default
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
sudo systemctl isolate rescue.target
Misconception check
Isolate switches immediately to a target and stops units not wanted by it; use set-default for persistent change.

screens.title: Create a simple custom service
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough builds the exact custom service described in the chapter. First create an executable script under /usr/local/bin that performs a simple long-running loop and writes to a logfile. Make it executable with chmod. Next create a service unit file under /etc/systemd/system with Unit, Service, and Install sections. In Service set ExecStart to the script path and Restart=always so systemd restarts the process when it exits. In Install set WantedBy=multi-user. target so enabling the unit ties it to the standard multi-user boot. After creating or updating unit files, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd reads the new configuration — this step is mandatory and a frequent omission. Start the service to validate it runs now, then enable it if you want it to start after reboot. Use systemctl status to confirm active state and journalctl -u to view the log entries your script writes. A common trap is forgetting file permissions on the script or using relative paths in ExecStart. Key takeaway: practice the full lifecycle — create, reload, start, enable, and inspect logs — to ensure your unit behaves predictably across reboots.

Start the service to validate it runs now, then enable it if you want it to start after reboot. Use systemctl status to confirm active state and journalctl -u to view the log entries your script writes. A common trap is forgetting file permissions on the script or using relative paths in ExecStart. Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Create custom service
Process

Step-by-step

  1. Create /usr/local/bin/mytestservice.sh and make it executable.
  2. Create /etc/systemd/system/mytestservice.service with Unit, Service, Install sections.
  3. Run sudo systemctl daemon-reload to register the new unit.
  4. Start and test with sudo systemctl start, then enable with sudo systemctl enable.
  5. Check status and use journalctl -u to follow logs and verify behavior.
Important
Always daemon-reload after creating or editing unit files, otherwise systemd will keep using the previous configuration.
Files to create
Script (/usr/local/bin/mytestservice.sh)
#!/bin/bash
LOGFILE="/var/log/mytestservice.log"
echo "$(date): My test service started." >> "$LOGFILE"
while true; do
  echo "$(date): My test service is running..." >> "$LOGFILE"
  sleep 10
done
Unit file (/etc/systemd/system/mytestservice.service)
[Unit]
Description=My Custom Test Service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mytestservice.sh
Restart=always
StandardOutput=syslog
StandardError=syslog
SyslogIdentifier=mytestservice

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Systemd workflows introduce a few repeatable traps that cause confusion during real work. The most frequent mistake is editing the wrong file: package-provided units under /usr/lib may be overwritten by updates, so place custom units or drop-ins under /etc or use systemctl edit which creates an override. Another common error is forgetting to run sudo systemctl daemon-reload after changing unit files; systemd continues using the cached unit definition until the daemon is reloaded. A third issue is expecting reload to always work: reload requests the service re-read its configuration, but not all daemons implement this behavior. If reload is unsupported, use restart. Also be careful with relative paths in ExecStart; always use absolute paths. For troubleshooting, collect evidence using systemctl status and journalctl -u, and inspect Main PID before killing or attaching a debugger. Concrete example: if a service fails after package upgrade, check whether the new packaged unit changed dependencies or environment variables before applying an override in /etc. Key takeaway: follow the safe workflow — use /etc for custom units or systemctl edit, run daemon-reload, verify with status and journalctl, then enable if persistent startup is required.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Common mistakes

Frequent pitfalls

  • Editing /usr/lib/systemd/system directly — use /etc or systemctl edit instead.
  • Forgetting sudo systemctl daemon-reload after changing unit files.
  • Assuming reload works for all services; when unsupported, restart is required.
  • Using relative paths in ExecStart; use absolute paths so systemd can find the executable.

Quick checklist

Make changes under /etc or create drop-ins with systemctl edit.
Run daemon-reload, then start the service and inspect status and journal entries.
Only enable after testing behavior across restarts.

screens.title: Unit dependency and ordering
screens.narratorSegment: Unit dependencies determine when systemd starts a unit relative to others. Two common dependency directives are Wants and Requires in the Unit section and After and Before to control ordering. Wants expresses a soft desire: the listed units are started if available but their failure will not stop the original unit. Requires is stronger: if a required unit fails to start, the depending unit also fails. After controls ordering without implying a dependency; it ensures the referenced unit is ordered earlier in startup. An example: if a service unit has Wants=network-online. target and After=network-online. target, systemd will attempt to start the network-online target and will order the service after it, but failure of the network-online target may not cause the service to fail unless Requires was used. Misconception: After does not automatically create a dependency; it only affects sequence. For deterministic startup, combine Wants/Requires with After so both ordering and dependency semantics are explicit. Practical significance: understanding these directives helps you avoid race conditions at boot and prevents services from starting before the resources they depend on are ready. Unit dependency and ordering means use wants/requires for dependency intent and after/before to set startup ordering; combine them for predictable boot sequencing.. In practical terms, how after= and wants= influence startup and failure handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Dependencies & Ordering
Hierarchy

Wants, Requires, After

Wants: soft dependency — start if available.
Requires: hard dependency — failure propagates.
After: ordering only, does not imply dependency.
Example
Unit: Wants=network-online.target After=network-online.target — attempts to start network-online and orders this unit after it, but does not fail on network failure unless Requires is used.

Practical tips

Combine Wants and After for best-effort ordering without causing cascade failures.
Use Requires only when the dependent unit absolutely must run for functionality.
When debugging boot order, inspect systemctl list-dependencies targetname to see relationships.

screens.title: Practical troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When a service fails to start, follow a concise troubleshooting workflow to gather evidence and act safely. Step one: run systemctl status unitname. service to get a snapshot of state, Main PID, and a recent log excerpt. Step two: run journalctl -u unitname. service with appropriate time filters to collect the full log stream and find error messages or stack traces. Step three: inspect the unit file and any overrides under /etc/systemd/system to ensure ExecStart, paths, and permissions are correct. Step four: confirm dependencies and ordering with systemctl list-dependencies and examine whether required units are active. Step five: if you modify unit files, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload and then restart the unit. Step six: repeat status and journal checks; if necessary, inspect the Main PID process with ps or check file permissions for the script or executable. A common misstep is restarting repeatedly without reading the journal — always collect logs first. Concrete example: if logs show a configuration parse error, open the service configuration file in the application, fix the syntax, and then restart. Key takeaway: follow an evidence-first approach and make one change at a time so you can measure its effect.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Troubleshooting workflow

Stepwise troubleshooting

1. Snapshot
systemctl status unitname.service — get active state and a log excerpt.
2. Full logs
journalctl -u unitname.service with time filters to gather full context.
3. Inspect unit
Check ExecStart, Restart, and Install sections in /etc or via systemctl cat.
4. Check deps
systemctl list-dependencies to confirm required units are active.
5. Reload rules
If unit changed, run daemon-reload then restart the unit and re-check logs.
6. Verify
Re-run status and journalctl. If unresolved, inspect process details or related configuration files.
Remember
Collect evidence before making changes and apply one change at a time so you can measure its impact.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of systemd and why it matters for day-to-day administration. Systemd is the init system that starts early in boot, manages services and sockets, evaluates dependencies, and maintains the journal of system events. You will learn the vocabulary systemd uses — units, service units, targets — and why those terms replace older runlevel concepts. We’ll also practice with systemctl commands to control services in the running session and to configure startup behavior for subsequent boots. Finally, we will create a small custom service so you see the full lifecycle: unit file, daemon reload, starting, enabling, and checking logs. This matters because most major distributions adopt systemd; competency with its commands and unit files is essential for reliably starting services, diagnosing failures, and automating startup behavior. By the end of the module you’ll be able to explain what a unit is, run basic systemctl workflows, and confidently handle common mistakes such as forgetting to run daemon-reload or editing package-provided unit files directly.

These objectives map to practical skills you must demonstrate. First, you will explain systemd's role and architecture, meaning you can describe why systemd runs early in boot and how it coordinates services and dependencies. A second objective is managing services with systemctl: you will start, stop, restart, reload, enable, and disable units reliably and understand the difference between the current running state and the enabled state for future boots. Third, you will identify common unit file types and locate unit files; you should be able to open a service unit and point out its sections and common directives. Fourth, you will understand targets and how they map to legacy runlevels so you can change the default target to a multi-user or graphical mode and explain rescue and emergency targets. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your mastery by performing the commands and explaining the results.

This second objectives screen links each skill to a concrete milestone. First, being able to explain systemd's architecture means you can describe units, the daemon, and how dependencies influence startup ordering. A milestone is to diagram a service's dependencies and explain why parallel startup speeds boot time. Second, for systemctl operations you should be able to start and stop a daemon, then enable it so it runs after reboot; the milestone is performing those commands and reporting the change in enabled state. Third, for unit files you will locate a service unit on disk, identify its Unit, Service, and Install sections, and explain common directives like ExecStart and Restart. The milestone is editing an override with systemctl edit rather than modifying packaged files. Fourth, for targets and logs you will show how to view the default target, change it, and use journalctl to collect a service's logs. The milestone is producing a journalctl export for a failed start. Each milestone is an actionable check you can perform in a lab environment.

Systemd is the init system and service manager used by most modern Linux distributions to orchestrate boot, services, and system-wide resources. At boot, systemd is the first user-space process the kernel launches. It reads unit files, determines dependencies, and brings up resources in a dependency-aware, parallel fashion so boot is faster and more predictable than older sequential init scripts. Units are the core abstraction: each unit file declares a resource and how to manage it. Service units describe daemons and how to start and stop them. Other unit types include mount for filesystems, socket for socket-activated services, timer for scheduled tasks, and target for grouping units into a logical state. Why this matters: when you understand systemd's role you can trace a failed boot to the responsible unit, adjust dependencies to control order, and use uniform tools to inspect state. A common misconception is thinking systemd only starts services; in fact it also manages the journal, socket activation, device activation, and timers. Example: if a network target is marked After for a web service, systemd will delay starting the web service until network. target is reached. Key takeaway: treat units as first-class objects you can query, modify, and reason about to control system behavior.

A unit is the primary object systemd manages. Each unit has a type and a unit file that describes how to start, stop, and configure that resource. The most common type you will edit is the service unit. Unit files are plain text with INI-like sections, typically Unit, Service, and Install for services. Unit file locations signal ownership and persistence: package-provided units generally live under /usr/lib/systemd/system, while system-wide customizations and overrides belong under /etc/systemd/system. When both locations define the same unit name, files in /etc take precedence. This is important because editing files under /usr/lib risks losing changes when packages update; instead, create drop-in overrides or place your unit in /etc. When you change unit files you must run daemon-reload to tell systemd to pick up the edits; failing to do so is a common error. Concrete example: a service unit contains ExecStart to start the daemon and Restart to control auto-restart behavior. Misconception check: people sometimes think enabling a service writes a startup script; in reality it creates symlinks under the selected target directories so systemd starts that unit when the target is active. Key takeaway: edit or override units in /etc and always reload the daemon after changes.

Systemctl is the primary tool for interacting with systemd. Use systemctl to change the current state of a unit and to alter whether it starts automatically in the future. The key commands you will use are start and stop to change the immediate running state, restart to stop and then start a service, and reload to request the service re-read its configuration without a full restart when supported. Another important pair is enable and disable: enable sets up the unit to start on matching targets after a reboot, and disable removes those startup links. A frequent confusion is treating start as persistent; starting a service affects only the current session — enabling controls future boots. Example scenario: you can start a web server to test a configuration change, and if it behaves correctly, enable it so it runs after reboot. Misconceptions often cause admins to forget enabling a service and be surprised after the next reboot. When reloading, check the service documentation to confirm it supports reload; otherwise use restart. Key takeaway: use start for immediate tests, enable for persistent startup, and daemon-reload whenever unit files change so systemctl acts on updated definitions.

When a service misbehaves, systemctl status is your first diagnostic tool. The status output summarizes whether a unit is active, its main PID, recent log lines forwarded from the journal, and runtime details such as memory usage. Learn to read three important pieces: the Active line shows state and timestamps, the Main PID line identifies the process you can inspect further, and the bottom log excerpt shows immediate errors and messages from the service or from systemd itself. Example: if status shows failed with a recent exit code and the log shows configuration parse errors, you know to inspect the unit's ExecStart and the service's configuration files. A common mistake is relying only on status; sometimes the status excerpt is too short. In that case use journalctl -u to view the full history. Also use systemctl show for machine-readable properties when you need environment variables or cgroup details. Practical tip: copy the unit name exactly and include the. service suffix for clarity when troubleshooting. Closing question: after reading status, what next step gives you the most evidence — checking journalctl for the full log or examining the unit file for misconfigured ExecStart arguments?

Journalctl is the central tool for viewing systemd's journal. For service troubleshooting, run journalctl with the -u flag followed by the unit name to see all entries for that service. You can limit output by time ranges or by following new entries in real time. For example, to see the most recent messages for a service you can run journalctl -u the service and then add --since to narrow to a timestamp range or -f to follow new lines. This helps when you restart a service and want to watch startup messages as they appear. A key point is that systemd aggregates logs from services and the kernel; journalctl gives you a unified timeline. Misconception: journalctl output can be large; use filtering flags and --no-pager to get machine-friendly output if you plan to pipe it. If you notice missing messages for a short-lived service, consider running journalctl -u with --since '5 minutes ago' immediately after a failure to capture ephemeral logs. Concrete example: to review only errors, pipe journalctl -u unitname --priority=err to focus on error-level messages. Closing thought: when in doubt, gather the journal as your primary evidence before editing unit files.

Targets offer a human-friendly way to express a set of units that should be active for a particular system state. They replace legacy runlevels with descriptive names like multi-user. target for non-graphical multi-user operation or graphical. target when a graphical session is desired. Rescue and emergency targets provide single-user and minimal states for recovery. Use systemctl get-default to see the default target the system boots into, and systemctl set-default to change it. Targets act as a collection point: enabling a target will pull in its WantedBy or Required units when the system reaches that target. A common misunderstanding is expecting targets to be services; instead they are grouping constructs — they do not run code but cause the units they reference to be started. Example: WantedBy=multi-user. target in a unit's Install section ensures the unit is started when multi-user. target becomes active. When troubleshooting boot state, examining which units a target requires and what failed during activation narrows the problem quickly. Key takeaway: change targets to alter boot behavior, but inspect unit dependencies to understand why a target fails to reach its desired state.

This hands-on walkthrough builds the exact custom service described in the chapter. First create an executable script under /usr/local/bin that performs a simple long-running loop and writes to a logfile. Make it executable with chmod. Next create a service unit file under /etc/systemd/system with Unit, Service, and Install sections. Let’s consolidate the essential ideas. First, systemd is the modern init and service manager that uses unit files and targets to orchestrate boot and service behavior. Second, units are the primary objects — service units describe how to start and manage daemons, and unit files are stored in locations that signal ownership; prefer /etc for your customizations. Third, systemctl is the single command-line interface you use to start, stop, restart, reload, enable, disable, and query units; remember start affects the current session while enable controls future boots. Fourth, journalctl provides unified logging for services and is your primary evidence source when troubleshooting. Finally, targets group units to form boot states that replace legacy runlevels. Keep these concepts handy when diagnosing failures and when writing unit files. Keep three compact reminders as you practice. First, always think in terms of units and targets rather than legacy scripts. Units are declarative and targets group them for boot states. Second, differentiate between immediate actions and persistent configuration: start, stop, and restart affect the running system; enable and disable change what happens at boot. Third, collect evidence: use systemctl status to capture state and journalctl -u to gather the full logs before making changes. These practices will reduce surprises during reboots and help you make safe, reversible modifications. When you face a failure, follow the workflow we practiced: status, journal, inspect unit and overrides, reload, restart, and re-verify. That sequence will get you to an informed fix quickly. What to Remember means think units → control with systemctl → verify with journalctl; use /etc for overrides and always daemon-reload after edits..
